headline: Upgrades route exclusively through staked-RAIL on-chain governance; uncontested fast path from callVote to executable is 7 days, with no multisig admin and no unilateral emergency override.

findings.text: Railgun proxy router 0xFA70…FA4b9 (PausableUpgradableProxy) reports owner() = Delegator 0xB6d5…fB53B; the Delegator reports owner() = Voting (Governor) 0xc480…A3CC at block 25086004–25086006. No EOA or multisig in the chain.

Upgradeability: the router is a custom PausableUpgradableProxy whose write surface (upgrade(address), pause(), unpause(), transferOwnership, changeFee, changeTreasury, addToBlocklist, setVerificationKey) is owner-gated; owner is the Delegator, whose owner is the Voting contract. Implementation pointer is live at 0xB4F2…D89b (verified, ABI source: etherscan) — the value differs from the address_book's older 0x3216… entry, evidence the proxy has been upgraded through governance.

Execution path: createProposal → 30-day sponsorship window (PROPOSAL_SPONSOR_THRESHOLD = 5e23 = 500,000 RAIL) → callVote → 2d review (VOTING_START_OFFSET = 172,800) → 3d yes/no vote (VOTING_YAY_END_OFFSET = 432,000) → 1d veto-only (VOTING_NAY_END_OFFSET = 518,400) → execution window opens at voteCallTime + EXECUTION_START_OFFSET = 604,800 s = 7 days and closes at EXECUTION_END_OFFSET = 1,209,600 s = 14 days. Uncontested fast-path delay from callVote to executable: 7 days. Executor: Voting.executeProposal which calls Delegator.callContract, which calls the target (proxy).

No multisig found in the upgrade path. There is no Safe, no proxy_admin EOA, no emergency council, and no separate guardian role on the Ethereum router. The address_book proxy_admin entry 0x4f8e…65c8 is not the proxy's owner per the live owner() read (owner is the Delegator).

Governance reads (block 25086006): QUORUM = 2e24 = 2,000,000 RAIL minimum 'yes' votes; PROPOSAL_SPONSOR_THRESHOLD = 5e23 = 500,000 RAIL; SPONSOR_WINDOW = 30 days; SPONSOR_LOCKOUT_TIME = 7 days; voting offsets are time-denominated (seconds), not block-denominated. STAKING_CONTRACT = 0xEE6A…Ee20 (staked-RAIL is the voting weight). Documentation corroborates: 2 M quorum, 500 k sponsorship, 2 d review + 3 d yes/no + 1 d veto + 1 d buffer + 7 d execution window.
No separate emergency-pause or guardian role distinct from governance. pause() and unpause() on the proxy are owner-gated → reachable only via the same 7-day governance path.

Highest reachable tier on the fast path is T1: upgrade(address) on the PausableUpgradableProxy can replace the implementation contract for the fund-custody router, and pause() can halt shield/transact/unshield flows. Reachable only through staked-RAIL governance with ≥7-day timelock between callVote and execution.

steelman.red: T1 powers (replace implementation, pause user flows) are reachable, and a coordinated attacker who acquires the 2 M RAIL quorum could push a malicious upgrade with no emergency veto multisig and no Security Council to intervene.
steelman.orange: The 7-day uncontested delay just meets the bar, fees are not bounded by any on-chain max in the changeFee signature, and there is no documented evidence of how broad the RAIL stake distribution actually is — concentration risk could collapse the governance protections.
steelman.green: All privileged write paths (upgrade, pause, fee, treasury, blocklist, verification key) require an on-chain proposal that cannot reach the executor until ≥7 days after callVote, weighted by staked RAIL with a 2 M-vote quorum, with no multisig admin, no EOA owner, and no unilateral emergency override.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the live on-chain reads show every upgrade and pause path terminating at the Voting contract via the Delegator, with EXECUTION_START_OFFSET = 7 days (604,800 s) — meeting the rubric's 'T1 reachable with uncontested-fast-path delay ≥7 days through active on-chain governance' anchor. The red steel-man (capture by 2 M RAIL) is the inherent risk of any token-governed protocol, not a feature of Railgun's design; the orange steel-man (just-at-bar, unverified distribution) is genuine but the protocol clears the timelock standard and there is no multisig shortcut that would otherwise force orange.

evidence.shows: PausableUpgradableProxy at router 0xFA70…FA4b9, owner() = Delegator 0xB6d5…fB53B, treasury() = 0xE8A8…fF40, live implementation = 0xB4F2…D89b (reads pinned to block 25086004); write surface includes upgrade, pause, unpause, changeFee, changeTreasury, addToBlocklist, setVerificationKey.
Delegator contract at 0xB6d5…fB53B reports owner() = 0xc480…A3CC; ABI exposes callContract(address,bytes,uint256) — the contract forwards arbitrary calls on behalf of its owner.

Voting (Governor) contract: DELEGATOR_CONTRACT = 0xB6d5…fB53B, STAKING_CONTRACT = 0xEE6A…Ee20, EXECUTION_START_OFFSET = 604800 s (7 d), EXECUTION_END_OFFSET = 1209600 s (14 d), VOTING_START_OFFSET = 172800 s (2 d), VOTING_YAY_END_OFFSET = 432000 s (5 d), VOTING_NAY_END_OFFSET = 518400 s (6 d), QUORUM = 2e24, PROPOSAL_SPONSOR_THRESHOLD = 5e23, SPONSOR_WINDOW = 2592000 s (30 d), SPONSOR_LOCKOUT_TIME = 604800 s (7 d), proposalsLength = 23. Reads pinned to block 25086006.

Protocol docs state: 'Any change to the smart contracts (including the governance, treasury, and voting contracts) requires the passing of an on-chain proposal. The decentralized governance system is the only way in which upgrades to the RAILGUN protocol can be made.' Documents the full pipeline (30-day sponsorship → 2-day review → 3-day vote → 1-day veto → 7-day execution window) corroborating on-chain reads.

unknowns: C5: token-distribution data for RAIL (top holders, staked supply, top-staker share) not verified this run; the 2 M-vote quorum's robustness depends on dispersion of staked balances.

C7: changeFee(uint120,uint120,uint256) on the router does not appear to enforce an on-chain upper bound in the visible ABI surface; verifying the implementation source for a max-fee constant would refine the T1/T2 classification of the fee surface — defaulted to T1 conservatively, but the highest tier is set by upgrade()/pause() regardless.

C1-polygon: did not separately fetch live owner()/delays for the Polygon governor 0xc3f2…aC88 or BSC governor 0xc3f2…aC88; per docs they are independent governance systems on RAILPOLY / RAILBSC tokens with the same architectural pattern.

admin_addresses.role: Delegator — executor forwarder, owned by the Voting contract

protocol_metadata.about: RAILGUN is a zero-knowledge privacy protocol that lets users shield ERC-20/ERC-721 tokens into a private balance tracked by Merkle commitments, then transact/unshield those tokens privately via zk-SNARK proofs without leaving the EVM chain. It is non-custodial smart-contract code (no separate chain, no bridge, no validator set), with a per-chain DAO governance system: staked RAIL on Ethereum governs the L1 and Arbitrum deployments, while RAILPOLY and RAILBSC govern Polygon and BSC independently.

headline: Exit (unshield) is permissionless and directly callable on-chain, but the proxy's pause() — reachable only through the 7-day on-chain governance vote — has no time cap and gates all user flows including claims.

findings.text: User-facing exit/transact functions on the router proxy 0xFA70…FA4b9 are transact(...) and shield(...) (and the fallback dispatch into the implementation). Unshielding is performed inside transact via the unshieldPreimage/UnshieldType field of the Transaction struct, with an Unshield(address,(uint8,address,uint256),uint256,uint256) event recording the recipient and amount. There is no separate two-step requestWithdrawal / claim pattern — exit is single-step, on-chain, and permissionless when not paused.

All user write functions (shield, transact) flow through the PausableUpgradableProxy's fallback dispatch. The proxy contract defines explicit pause()/unpause() functions that disable that dispatch — when paused, both shield and transact (which contains unshield) revert. There is no distinct exit-only function that bypasses pause.

Pause role: pause()/unpause() on the proxy are owner-gated; owner is the Delegator 0xB6d5…fB53B, whose owner is the Voting contract 0xc480…A3CC. Pause is therefore reachable only by an on-chain proposal completing the ≥7-day governance pipeline. There is no maximum pause duration encoded in the ABI; ProxyPause/ProxyUnpause events show pause is a binary state, not auto-expiring.

No separate emergency-pause path exists distinct from the slow governance route. There is no guardian multisig, no time-capped emergency role, and no gate-seal committee on the Ethereum router; the only pause actor is the same governance executor that performs upgrades.
Queued redemption: not applicable — unshielding is single-tx finalization within transact, not a request-and-claim queue. There is no daily withdrawal cap or per-block throttle visible in the ABI.
No forced-exit / escape-hatch / permissionless emergency-exit mechanism. Pause is binary and is the only failure mode; there is no fallback that lets users withdraw if governance pauses indefinitely.

transact and shield are public, non-payable functions on the verified proxy implementation and are directly callable from any EVM client (Etherscan write tab, ethers/web3, the RAILGUN SDK, or third-party wallets like Railway Wallet). No frontend dependency for exit; the SDK and multiple wallets are documented in the Railgun ecosystem.

steelman.red: Pause has no time cap; a passed governance proposal can permanently freeze unshielding, meeting the rubric's 'ANY actor (including governance) can pause CLAIMS of finalized exits indefinitely' clause.
steelman.orange: Pause is indefinite but is reachable only through a 7-day token-weighted vote with 2 M-RAIL quorum, not via any unilateral admin or multisig — matching the rubric's 'orange = indefinite pause is reachable only through governance vote (not unilateral admin action)'.
steelman.green: Exit is single-step, permissionless, has no queue, and works from any wallet without the Railgun frontend — but green is unreachable while pause(any-scope, no-time-cap) sits in the contract and gates the unshield path.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because pause is indefinite (no auto-expiry, no time cap in the ABI) AND it gates the exit flow, but it is actuated only by the same 7-day on-chain governance pipeline as upgrades — never by an EOA, multisig, or guardian. The red steel-man would force red if a unilateral admin or short-quorum multisig held the pause; here the actor is staked-RAIL governance with a ≥7-day delay, which is the orange criterion.

evidence.shows: Router proxy ABI exposes pause(), unpause(), and upgrade(address) under the proxy admin's control, plus Unshield(address,...) event signature confirming on-chain unshield path; owner() = Delegator (per same fetch).

Current implementation (verified on Etherscan) exposes transact(Transaction[]) and shield(ShieldRequest[]) as the public state-mutating functions, with no whitelist modifier on either. The Unshield event with recipient/amount confirms unshielding happens inside transact.
Delegator owner() = Voting contract 0xc480…A3CC, confirming pause()/upgrade() on the router are only reachable via Voting.executeProposal → Delegator.callContract.
Confirms all changes (including pause-equivalent calls into the router) require passing the full sponsorship→vote→veto→7-day-execution governance pipeline.

unknowns: E5: did not verify on-chain whether the implementation contains an internal whenNotPaused gate at the function-body level vs only at the proxy fallback boundary — practically equivalent here because all user functions go through the proxy dispatch, but the precise revert site was not read.

headline: Self-contained zk-SNARK shield/unshield system with no oracle, no bridge, no off-chain reporter committee, and no keeper-liveness dependency; impacted TVS under any single external-dependency failure is effectively <1%.

findings.text: External contract calls in the verified router/implementation ABI: none of price-oracle, AMM-pool, lending-pool, or yield-wrapper character. The contract reads/writes only its own internal Merkle-tree state, the ERC-20s being shielded, and a verifying-key registry for SNARK verification. Grep targets (latestAnswer, getPrice, chainlink, pyth, redstone) return no method on the merged ABI.

No off-chain reporter committee. There is no exit-bus, no oracle-poster set, no fraud-prover, no DAO-selected validator set acting as a protocol reporter. Verifying keys are governance-set via setVerificationKey, not committee-reported per round.

Bridge dependencies: Ethereum L1 deployment has no bridge in its critical path. Arbitrum L2 deployment uses the L1Sender (0x20Fa…3bD5) → L2Executor (0xc480…A3CC) pattern documented for cross-layer governance only — it carries governance messages from Ethereum to Arbitrum, not user funds. Polygon and BSC have their own independent governance and tokens; they are not dependent on Ethereum for fund custody.

No nested collateral / restaking chain. Railgun wraps user-deposited ERC-20s 1:1 into Merkle-commitment notes; there is no receipt-of-receipt structure, no slashing power at any level, and no rebasing/yield mechanism that propagates third-party failure into Railgun's accounting.
Fork lineage: not stated in any fetched source; the protocol is documented as an original zk-SNARK construction. No finding to record.

Fallback mechanisms: the protocol exposes snarkSafetyVector / checkSafetyVectors and a tokenBlocklist as on-chain safety surfaces; these are LIVE and enforcing on-chain (governance can add/remove blocked tokens and safety vectors via the same 7-day pipeline). They are admin-style guards, not external-dependency fallbacks, because there are no external dependencies that need fallbacks.

Sequencer/L1-liveness dependency beyond substrate: none. Railgun is not its own appchain; on each chain it inherits that chain's substrate. The Ethereum deployment depends only on Ethereum L1; the Arbitrum/Polygon/BSC deployments depend only on those chains' substrates. A7 does not fire.

Keeper / relayer liveness: Railgun's relayer network (used to forward shielded transactions while paying gas in shielded tokens for user privacy) is PERMISSIONLESS and OPTIONAL — a user can submit transact() directly from any wallet without a relayer. If all relayers disappear, users lose the privacy convenience of fee-paying-in-shielded-tokens, but neither principal nor unclaimed yield is at risk and exits remain callable directly. Failure mode is graceful.

Governance-mutable external dependency surface: setVerificationKey can replace the SNARK verifying key (a self-internal dependency, not an external one); addToBlocklist/removeFromBlocklist controls which ERC-20s are shieldable. Neither swaps in a new external oracle, bridge, or third-party vault. The router does not reference an upgradable router/registry that would let governance silently introduce a new external contract into the user-funds flow. A9 does not fire in its scope-limited form (admin upgrade authority is a CONTROL-slice concern, captured there).

steelman.red: Governance can replace the verifying key via setVerificationKey, and a backdoored key could theoretically let an attacker forge proofs and drain shielded funds — though this is governance-internal, not an external dependency.
steelman.orange: The protocol relies on Ethereum's BN254 pairing precompiles and on the soundness of the trusted setup for its SNARK; a precompile change or trusted-setup leak would degrade privacy/security guarantees, though neither has historically broken users' principal.
steelman.green: No oracles, no bridges, no committees, no keepers required for solvency, no nested collateral. The shield/unshield math is self-contained and verified on-chain via the BN254 precompile; external failures cannot cause loss of principal.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the inspected ABI and docs show no external-dependency surface in the user-funds flow: no oracle reads, no cross-chain message bus carrying TVL, no committee finalizing withdrawals, no keeper required for solvency. Impacted TVS under any single external dependency failure is effectively <1% (essentially zero — there are no qualifying external dependencies). The red steel-man is a control-slice risk (governance-mutable verifying key) re-cast as autonomy, which the slice explicitly excludes; the orange steel-man (precompile/trusted-setup) is base-chain substrate.

evidence.shows: Merged router/implementation ABI contains no oracle, bridge, or external-protocol-call signatures; state-mutating functions are shield, transact, plus admin-only changeFee/changeTreasury/addToBlocklist/setVerificationKey. View methods touch only Merkle state, fees, and verifying keys.

Docs state RAILGUN 'is 100% non-custodial' and 'no centralized control, no extra validators, and no trusted bridges' — corroborates the absence of external dependencies for solvency; relayers are described as a privacy convenience, not a custody requirement.

unknowns: A8: did not independently verify on-chain that there is no implicit relayer-gated path (e.g., a relayer-signed adapter contract referenced by adaptContract in BoundParams); the relayer-permissionless claim rests on the ABI shape plus docs, not on a deep code-walk of the implementation source.

A3-bridge-multichain: did not separately fetch the Polygon/BSC routers' ABIs this run to confirm they have no cross-chain bridge in the user-funds path; structurally they are described as independent deployments, but on-chain verification of those chains is deferred.

headline: shield/transact/unshield have no whitelist, no KYC, and no operator-approval gate; the protocol is reachable through a published SDK and multiple independent wallet apps (Railway, others) without the Railgun publisher's frontend.

findings.text: No whitelist/allowlist/onlyRole/onlyKYC modifier on user-facing entry points. shield(ShieldRequest[]) and transact(Transaction[]) on the proxy implementation 0xB4F2…D89b have no caller restriction — anyone holding the underlying ERC-20 (and a valid SNARK proof for transact) can call them.

No off-chain operator approval is required for admission. Relayers may optionally forward a transact() to provide gas abstraction and metadata privacy, but the function admits a self-submitted call from any EOA. There is no privileged poster, sequencer, or gated relayer set.

Frontend restrictions: did not retrieve verbatim ToS text from railgun.org in this run (the fetched landing page returned only metadata tags), so A3-passive vs A3-active classification is left to A6 below. Even if the official frontend imposes geo-blocking or ToS clauses, those are publisher-side and not contract-level.

Independent access paths exist: (i) the Railway Wallet (independent mobile wallet developed by a separate entity, reachable on iOS/Android) integrates Railgun for end-users without using a Railgun-operated frontend; (ii) the RAILGUN SDK / engine packages (referenced in docs as the developer entry point) let any developer interact with the contracts directly; (iii) docs explicitly state 'Independent wallet providers can use the RAILGUN protocol' and link to a list of wallet providers. Any of these constitutes a separate publisher path.

Sanctions/compliance tooling at the contract level: the router contains a tokenBlocklist(address) mapping with addToBlocklist/removeFromBlocklist admin calls — this is a TOKEN-level filter (which ERC-20s can be shielded), not a USER blocklist. There is no addr→bool blocklist over wallets, no OFAC/Chainalysis oracle wired into shield/transact.

Read vs write: all view methods on the router/implementation are public-callable (read-permissionless); the state-mutating user functions (shield, transact) are also unrestricted at the caller level. Admin write methods (changeFee, addToBlocklist, etc.) are owner-only and that ownership chain is the Delegator → Voting contract.

ToS / Legal clauses: did not extract verbatim ToS text from railgun.org in this run — the landing page fetch returned only OpenGraph meta-tags, not the body content. ToS posture is therefore recorded in unknowns rather than asserted.

steelman.red: If the official frontend enforces active wallet screening or geo-blocking and no real independent path existed, the protocol would be operationally captured by the publisher — but the SDK and Railway Wallet rebut this.
steelman.orange: tokenBlocklist gives governance an admission-style gate over which assets can be shielded, and the official frontend's ToS posture is not verified in this run, leaving a small chance that operational reachability is narrower than the contract surface suggests.
steelman.green: Contracts are fully permissionless on shield/transact/unshield with no caller-side whitelist, no KYC, no on-chain user blocklist, and no off-chain operator gate; an independent wallet (Railway) and an SDK both exist as separate publisher paths, satisfying the A3b independent-path test.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because (a) both core user actions (shield via shield(...) and exit via transact(...) with unshieldPreimage) are caller-unrestricted on the verified implementation, and (b) at least one independent A3b path exists (Railway Wallet as a separately-operated frontend, plus the RAILGUN SDK as a published developer library). Per the slice's default-grade guidance, frontend ToS and publisher-side enforcement are reported as context and do not block green when contracts are permissionless and an independent path exists. tokenBlocklist is a token-asset gate, not a user-admission gate, and does not affect this grade.

evidence.shows: Implementation ABI: shield(ShieldRequest[]) and transact(Transaction[]) carry no access modifiers in the function inputs/signature (no caller param check, no role parameter, no whitelist mapping argument); tokenBlocklist mapping is asset-keyed (address→bool), not user-keyed.

Docs state 'Independent wallet providers can use the RAILGUN protocol, head here to select from a list of wallet providers' and 'RAILGUN is 100% non-custodial' — confirms independent-frontend pathway and absence of custodial gating.

unknowns: A6: did not retrieve verbatim ToS text from railgun.org in this run (the landing page fetch returned only OpenGraph meta-tags); A3-passive vs A3-active classification of the official frontend is therefore not assertable from evidence and is recorded here rather than in findings.

A3b: did not fetch a specific Railway Wallet or SDK URL this run — the independent-path claim rests on Railgun docs' description of independent wallet providers (cited above) plus widely-corroborated search-engine evidence of Railway Wallet's existence; deeper-evidence of a non-Railgun-operated frontend is deferred to a future run.

headline: Proxy, current implementation, Delegator and Voting contracts are all verified on Etherscan; protocol has been audited by Trail of Bits, Zokyo, ABDK and others, with on-chain upgrade history matching the audited proxy pattern.
short_headline: All core contracts verified; ToB+Zokyo audits

findings.text: Router proxy 0xFA70…FA4b9 — abiSource = etherscan (verified); current implementation 0xB4F2…D89b auto-resolved from the proxy slot — abiSource = etherscan (verified); Delegator 0xB6d5…fB53B — verified; Voting contract 0xc480…A3CC — verified. Reads at blocks 25086004–25086010 confirm all four core contracts return a parseable, source-resolved ABI.

Public source repositories Railgun-Privacy and Railgun-Community are referenced in the protocol context and are widely documented as the canonical code. The ABIs returned by the read API match the expected shape of the PausableUpgradableProxy / RailgunLogic / Delegator / Voting contracts described in Railgun's docs and the Zokyo Nov-2021 audit. A specific deploy-commit SHA-to-implementation bytecode match was not independently produced this run — recorded as a scope note, not a downgrade trigger.

Audit coverage: pinned audit_links reference Zokyo (Nov 2021, RailgunLogic) and ABDK (Jul 2021). Search-grounded sources (Trail of Bits' own publications page; the Trustblock AMA) confirm Trail of Bits audited Railgun in Feb 2022 (level-of-effort 4) and that multiple subsequent audits (Hacken, Pessimistic, Hashcloak, additional Zokyo engagements) have been performed, with 'at least seven audits over two years' as of Dec 2024.

Auditor recognition: Trail of Bits and Zokyo are explicitly on the slice's recognized-firm list; Hacken is also recognized. ABDK is a respected cryptography-specialist firm widely used for zk circuits but is not on the slice's named list — corroborative rather than primary. Naming convention satisfied via the ToB and Zokyo engagements.

Post-audit drift: the on-chain implementation 0xB4F2…D89b is newer than the address_book's older 0x3216…e13b implementation, confirming the proxy has been upgraded via governance since the original audits. Whether the drift since the most recent audit is material (new functions, changed access control, accounting changes) was not diffed this run — recorded in unknowns rather than auto-downgrading, per V5 'sample the diff content before claiming material drift' guidance.

Implementation vs proxy: implementation 0xB4F2…D89b is verified separately from the proxy 0xFA70…FA4b9 (both report abiSource = etherscan independently). The proxy is a custom PausableUpgradableProxy pattern, not a generic ERC1967 — its source is what was directly audited by Zokyo.

steelman.red: If the deployed bytecode at 0xB4F2…D89b had no public source on Etherscan or the audits all predated the current implementation with no follow-up, the protocol would be effectively unverified — but neither condition holds.
steelman.orange: The implementation has been upgraded since the original Zokyo Nov-2021 audit and a precise diff-coverage match between the most recent audit's commit and the live bytecode was not produced in this run, so a small chance of unreviewed drift in fund-custody code remains.
steelman.green: Both proxy and current implementation are verified on Etherscan, the source-repo structure is well-known (Railgun-Privacy / Railgun-Community), and the protocol has multiple audits from recognized firms (Trail of Bits Feb-2022, Zokyo multiple, Hacken) with ongoing review.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the V1/V6 conditions are met (proxy and implementation independently verified), V3/V4 are met (Trail of Bits and Zokyo, both recognized firms, have audited the protocol — plus Hacken and ABDK), and V2 has a recognized public repo whose contents correspond to the explorer-visible source. V5 drift is recorded as an unknown rather than evidence of degradation, consistent with the slice's guidance that commit-count alone is not a finding.

evidence.shows: Router proxy 0xFA70…FA4b9 — 'ABI source: etherscan', PausableUpgradableProxy, proxy → 0xB4F2…D89b auto-resolved.
Implementation 0xB4F2…D89b — 'ABI source: etherscan' confirming verified bytecode; full RailgunLogic ABI including shield/transact/changeFee/upgrade pattern is visible.
Delegator 0xB6d5…fB53B — 'ABI source: etherscan' (verified); ABI matches the documented Delegator contract pattern.
Voting (Governor) 0xc480…A3CC — 'ABI source: etherscan' (verified); ABI matches the documented governance pattern.

Zokyo's Nov 2021 audit of RailgunLogic: 'There were no critical issues found during the audit … Only the governance process can change the deployed code (Proxy pattern).' Confirms the audited contract is the same architectural pattern deployed today.
Trail of Bits' own publications index lists 'RAILGUN · Feb 2022 · 4' as a level-of-effort-4 engagement, confirming the protocol has been audited by a V4-recognized firm post-deployment.

unknowns: V2: did not pin a specific deploy-commit SHA for the live implementation 0xB4F2…D89b nor produce a local bytecode-match in this run; the implementation/repo correspondence rests on architectural-shape match (function set, events, modifiers) rather than a hash-identical compile.

V5: did not diff the most recent recognized-firm audit's pinned commit against the bytecode at 0xB4F2…D89b — drift extent (new functions vs refactors) is not characterized; the protocol's docs cite continual review and ≥7 audits over 2 years as of Dec 2024, but the specific delta covered by each is not enumerated here.

V3: did not fetch the pinned audit_links directly this run (the .ch host in the protocol context is non-canonical; the canonical assets.railgun.org/docs/audits/ index was surfaced via search rather than a direct GET) — Zokyo Nov-2021 and ToB Feb-2022 are corroborated through search-grounded sources rather than direct PDF fetches.
